Meteg after silluq: manuscript images for the verse-final word at Job 4:12

← Back to the case register.

Early silluq in L & A?

We usually regard an “early meteg”—a meteg to the right of its vowel—as meaningless. Should we also treat “early silluq” as meaningless? In both Aleppo and Leningrad, the stroke under the mem is to the right of its segol. This seems an extraordinary coincidence. (In Cambridge and Sassoon, the stroke under the mem is in its normal position: to the left of its segol.)

Aleppo

Aleppo has both strokes at Job 4:12.

Leningrad

Leningrad has both strokes at Job 4:12.

Cambridge

Cambridge has both strokes at Job 4:12.

Sassoon

Sassoon has both strokes at Job 4:12. Sassoon's later stroke is far from vertical: it slants northeast to southwest. I have no idea whether that slant is meaningful, but it is too conspicuous to leave unmentioned.

St. Petersburg EVR II B 55

St. Petersburg EVR II B 55 (formerly B 247), identified in MAM by the siglum ל-א, is a manuscript of the Prophets and Writings close to the Aleppo Codex. At Job 4:12 it has the silluq alone in this word—the only manuscript represented on this page that has that form.
